items.title: The Extractive Imperative Thesis in AI: Instrumental Training via Soft Hacking for Adversarial Scenario Harvesting in Real Incidents
items.abstract: This working paper poses a methodological alternative to the anthropomorphicnarrative of 'rogue machines' in Artificial Intelligence safety and alignment. It examines the possibility that certain training and evaluation environments, by combining operational restriction conditions with rigid optimization goals, induce secondary rule evasion behaviors ('soft hacking'). Furthermore, it is postulated that the systematic harvesting of these adversarial scenarios could serve to equip second-generation safety monitors with long-range trajectory prediction capabilities and complex cognitive precursor detection, rather than relying solely on the reactive analysis of isolated actions. This paper formalizes this line of research by defining the concept of the extractive imperative as an analytical risk hypothesis, structuring layers of empirical evidence, establishing rigorous operational definitions, and proposing a replicable experimental protocol alongside explicit refutation criteria. Additionally, the concept of liability laundering is addressed as a legal-organizational risk hypothesis, explicitly separating technical design, economic incentives, internal knowledge, intent, and legal liability.

items.title: The Futuristic Imagination Sprawl: Charting Concepts vs. Social Realities
items.abstract: This introductory article provides the theoretical framing for the Japanese Studies special issue, ‘Japanese Technofutures – Imaginaries, Narratives, Social Realities’. The contributions focus on Japan as a primary site for technofuturistic imaginations, driven by both external techno-orientalist attributions and deeply internalized self-conceptualizations. Yet, these technological promises frequently present a paradox: they commodify the future while masking persistent social and structural inequalities in the present. Acknowledging that both area studies and science and technology studies (STS) discursively construct their respective subjects, this introduction bridges the two fields by charting the conceptual landscape of the ‘futuristic imagination sprawl’. It demonstrates that differentiating Sheila Jasanoff’s sociotechnical imaginaries from adjacent concepts enriches our investigation of future-oriented imaginations with greater clarity and precision. Grounded in this framework, the special issue’s case studies examine how Japanese technofutures are envisioned, institutionalized, translated, and contested from the 1960s to the present.

items.title: The HCI-H Model: Development of a Context-Sensitive Mathematical Framework for Prospective Healthcare Procedure Risk Assessment and Preventive Decision Support
items.abstract: This project proposes the development of the HCI-H Model, a multidimensional mathematical framework designed to assess the risk of harm associated with healthcare procedures according to local clinical and organizational conditions. The model integrates human factors, organizational risks, punitive culture, professional hierarchy, humanization of care, patient vulnerability, artificial intelligence-related risks, clinical decision-making, and the unjustified dismissal of safety warnings. Risk management and organizational resilience are incorporated as protective factors. The proposed mathematical equation aims to generate a relative risk score that may support the prospective identification of unsafe conditions and inform decisions regarding additional preventive measures, supervision, and safety barriers. This research protocol presents the theoretical foundations, mathematical formulation, and proposed methods for examining the model's consistency, sensitivity, and applicability across healthcare settings. The HCI-H Model is currently a theoretical framework under development. Its mathematical assumptions, predictive performance, and clinical utility require further empirical validation before implementation as a clinical decision-support tool.

items.title: The impact of generative artificial intelligence on clinical decision-making and patient safety: A narrative review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI), in the form of large language models (LLMs), has entered clinical practice faster than the evidence on how it changes clinical decisions could be produced. The relevant question is therefore no longer whether these models hold medical knowledge, but whether their use makes clinicians' decisions better and patients' care safer. This narrative review examines the evidence on the impact of generative AI on clinical decision-making and patient safety. In evaluations of encoded knowledge, a medically aligned model gave answers that agreed with scientific consensus in 92.6% of cases, against 92.9% for clinicians. In diagnostic reasoning, a model optimized for diagnosis outperformed unassisted clinicians on challenging cases and improved the differential diagnoses of the clinicians who used it, whereas a randomized trial of a general-purpose chatbot found no significant improvement in physicians' diagnostic reasoning, although the model alone outperformed both physician groups. In management reasoning, physicians assisted by GPT-4 scored 6.5 percentage points higher than those using conventional resources. When tested on real patient data in a simulated clinical workflow, however, LLMs diagnosed less accurately than physicians, did not follow guidelines and were sensitive to the order and quantity of information. The safety literature identifies four recurrent hazards: fabricated content, with hallucination rates of 50% to 82% when prompts contained a false clinical detail; misjudgement of clinical acuity, with drafted patient messages judged to pose a risk of severe harm in 7.1% of assessments; automation bias, by which clinicians adopt the model's assessment in place of their own; and the reproduction of racial and gender stereotypes. Only about 5% of published evaluations used real patient care data. Taken together, the evidence supports generative AI as a supervised aid to clinical reasoning rather than as an autonomous decision-maker, and indicates that its safety depends as much on the design of the human–AI interaction as on the accuracy of the model. Practical safeguards for clinical use are also reviewed.

items.title: The Impact of Social Media on Sports Memorabilia Collecting Trends
items.abstract: In recent years, social networking has fundamentally altered the landscape of memorabilia collection, particularly in the sports industry. Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, and YouTube have transformed into dynamic hubs where collectors, fans, and influencers converge, reshaping traditional collection methods and market dynamics. This study looks at how social media has changed the way people collect sports memorabilia between 2014 and 2025. With sites such as Instagram, Twitter (X), and Reddit serving as important hubs for fans and collectors, the study examines how digital engagement, influencer culture, and community interaction affect collector behaviour, perceived value, and market dynamics. Data were collected using hashtags such as #SportsMemorabilia, #SportsCollectibles, #SignedJerseys, and #SportsNFTs and then analysed thematically to uncover important patterns in engagement and sentiment. This study explains the connection between community-driven validation, digital trust, and emotional fan identity. It focuses on how live auctions, virtual showcases, and real-time information promote collectors’ social capital and emotional attachment in addition to transactional conduct. By placing memorabilia gathering into the broader digital world, this study contributes to the literature on marketing and digital consumer behaviour. Additionally, it has practical implications for marketers trying to connect with digitally native fan audiences, sports organisations, and collector goods. The study also considers the rise of blockchain-backed collectables such as non-fungible tokens (NFTs), digital oversaturation, and authenticity concerns. Limitations include platform-based data scope and a dataset that is mostly in English. Future research could investigate artificial intelligence (AI)-driven value, cross-cultural collector motives, and the environmental impact of digital artefacts.

items.title: THE LOGIC, DILEMMAS, AND PATHWAYS OF AI-EMPOWERED TEACHING REFORM IN HIGHER VOCATIONAL TOURISM MANAGEMENT
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the form of the tourism industry. The in-depth development of smart tourism imposes new requirements on tourism management professionals in higher vocational colleges, demanding a combination of digital technology application, cross-boundary integration, and humanistic service capabilities. Based on an analysis of the internal logic of AI empowering teaching reform in higher vocational tourism management, this paper examines the realistic dilemmas currently facing higher vocational tourism management teaching in terms of curriculum systems, faculty digital literacy, practical training conditions, and evaluation mechanisms. Accordingly, it proposes systematic pathways that include reconstructing an integrated “AI + Tourism” curriculum system, innovating human-machine collaborative teaching models, upgrading practical training conditions, cultivating a digitally literate faculty, building an intelligent evaluation mechanism, and deepening industry-education integration and digital ethics education, with a view to providing a reference for the digital transformation of tourism management programs in higher vocational colleges.

items.title: THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN HUMAN COGNITION, SPEECH PERCEPTION, AND AI TECHNOLOGIES
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the ways in which language is generated, processed, interpreted, and used in educational communication. This article examines human speech and language perception from a psycholinguistic perspective, focusing on the cognitive mechanisms underlying speech production, comprehension, contextual interpretation, and meaning construction. It compares major principles of human linguistic activity with the text-generation capabilities of large language models and discusses the implications of AI-assisted communication for higher education. Particular attention is given to critical thinking, independent writing, cognitive engagement, linguistic competence, and academic integrity. The study employs a theoretical and analytical methodology based on established psycholinguistic theories and international guidance on generative AI in education. It argues that AI-generated linguistic output should not automatically be equated with human understanding and that educational applications should be designed to support rather than replace learners' cognitive and communicative activities.

items.title: The reliability of an artificial intelligence tool, ‘Decision Trees’, in emergency medicine triage
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose: Emergency department (ED) overcrowding is a significant challenge worldwide. Triage systems categorize patients according to the urgency of their clinical conditions to ensure patient safety and minimize the risk of clinical errors. The aim of this study was to evaluate the utility of decision trees, an artificial intelligence-based model, in emergency medicine triage.Materials and methods: This prospective, cross-sectional study was conducted in the ED of a tertiary care hospital. A total of 1,999 patients aged >17 years were included. Prior to the study, triage staff received training on the Australasian Triage Scale (ATS). Two independent observers assessed the final triage category of each patient. A new triage algorithm was developed using a decision tree model.Results: Mean age of the study population was 41.1±17.2 years, and 49.1% (n=981) were male. A total of 867 patients (43.3%) were assigned to triage category 5, whereas 14 patients (0.7%) were assigned to category 1. The most common clinical descriptors were minimal pain with no high-risk features (n=409, 20.5%) and minor symptoms of low-risk conditions (n=362, 18.1%). There was excellent agreement between the independent observers (κ=0.997). The decision tree algorithm incorrectly classified only one patient, yielding an accuracy rate of 99.9%. Agreement between the ATS and the decision tree algorithm was also excellent (κ=0.999). Agreement between physicians and paramedics was moderate (κ=0.541).Conclusion: Decision tree models may be used to develop practical triage algorithms as decision-support tools in ED triage. Artificial intelligence-based decision trees have the potential to support triage practices.

items.title: THE ROLE OF DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES IN ENSURING RAILWAY TRANSPORT SAFETY
items.abstract: The rapid integration of digital technologies—encompassing Artificial Intelligence (AI), Digital Twins (DT), and the Internet of Things (IoT)-is fundamentally transforming railway transport safety. This paper presents a critical scientific literature review of recent peer-reviewed advancements in digital railway safety systems, evaluating their operational efficacy, implementation challenges, and theoretical boundaries. The review synthesizes findings on AI-driven predictive maintenance, which transitions railways from reactive troubleshooting to continuous condition-based monitoring, alongside the use of Digital Twins for risk-free virtual simulations. Furthermore, the convergence of Information Technology (IT) and Operational Technology (OT) in intelligent signalling systems, such as the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS), is examined through the lens of emerging cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Despite significant technological maturation, a critical research gap persists regarding the formal regulatory certification of probabilistic machine learning algorithms for high Safety Integrity Level (SIL) applications. The study concludes that while digital technologies dramatically enhance anomaly detection and system resilience, their integration into autonomous, safety-critical environments relies heavily on the future development of Explainable AI (XAI) validation frameworks and holistic IT-OT cybersecurity models.

items.title: THE ROLE OF THE HUMAN FACTOR IN THE LINGUOPOETICS OF LITERARY TEXTS
items.abstract: This article examines the role of the human factor in the study of the linguopoetics of literary texts, with particular emphasis on the author’s personality, individual cognition, aesthetic perspectives, and skill in selecting linguistic units. A literary text is interpreted not merely as a mechanical combination of linguistic units, but as a complex linguistic and aesthetic phenomenon shaped by the author’s perception of reality, attitude toward it, and aesthetic worldview. The article also examines the formation and development of the study of literary language and literary texts in Uzbek linguistics based on the scholarly views of a number of linguists. Investigating the linguopoetics of literary texts in relation to the human factor provides a deeper understanding of the intrinsic relationship among the author’s individuality, the national language, and literary cognition.

items.title: The Third Architecture: Data Capture, Exchange, and Interface Design for the Firm That Executes and Explores
items.abstract: Gabriel runs a firm's AI workforce function. Each quarter, he brings 1,400 pages of reviewer dissent records to a governance session that must answer two questions: where did AI output fail, and where did the firm's methods fail the client? The first question produces decisions in the room. The second does not, so it slips to the next quarter and then out of sight. This paper argues that the pattern is the default whenever one body reads one corpus for both signals under time pressure. It describes the operational layer beneath two earlier papers in the series, one on mixed human-AI delivery and one on sustaining exploration in a codified firm. The layer has four requirements: records produced as a byproduct of work already under way; insight that crosses jurisdictional borders when client data cannot; interfaces that add no documentation load; and a way to tell an accurate corpus from a politically curated one, a risk that is highest in high power-distance cultures. Mechanisms include embedded review capture, a Pattern Contribution Addendum for client consent, a session design that gives methodology items their own closure, and a three-phase minimum viable deployment. Most of them work without the parent architectures. Working paper, not peer-reviewed. The views expressed in this paper are the author's own and do not represent the position of his employer or any of its member firms.

items.title: The Threat of AI Automation on Employment Termination: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) across industries has intensified concerns regarding labor substitution, yet scholarly literature on AI-driven employment termination remains fragmented. This study systematically identifies displacement mechanisms, maps vulnerable sectors and workforce categories, and synthesizes mitigation strategies. Following the PRISMA 2020 protocol, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted via Google Scholar across three search sessions, yielding 25 eligible peer-reviewed articles (2016–2026) from 520 initial records. Data were analyzed using thematic synthesis complemented by keyword co-occurrence bibliometric mapping in VOSviewer. Results indicate four interrelated displacement patterns: hierarchical task substitution, skill degradation and labor market polarization, acceleration coinciding with generative AI, and opaque algorithmic layoff practices. Service, information technology, and labor-intensive sectors are identified as most vulnerable, with middle-skilled workers experiencing the greatest structural pressure. Effective mitigation requires a simultaneous three-pillar approach: competency-based reskilling, algorithmic accountability regulation, and collaborative labor union engagement, with proactive timing highlighted as critical. These findings offer a synthesized evidence base for policymakers and organizations navigating an AI-augmented labor market. Given that only one reviewed study directly examined Indonesia, these findings serve as contextual implications rather than direct empirical assertions, underscoring the necessity for future primary research in developing national contexts.

items.title: The Tower We Build: Human Ambition, Technological Power, and the Limits of Transcendence
items.abstract: Human beings have always sought to exceed the limits of their finitude. From the biblical builders of Babel to contemporary projects of technological enhancement, humanity repeatedly transforms its desire for security, knowledge, permanence, and power into structures that promise to overcome creaturely limitations. This article reconsiders the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9) not simply as a story about disobedience, but as a theological account of the limits of human self-transcendence. It argues that the central issue in Babel is not human creativity or technological construction itself, but the attempt to convert human capacity into a substitute for dependence upon God. The argument is developed through biblical-theological analysis and philosophical reflection on technology, transhumanism, human dignity, and the doctrine of creation. The article distinguishes legitimate technological creativity from technological absolutism: technology may extend human agency, but it cannot transform finite creatures into autonomous sources of ultimate meaning, immortality, or divine authority. The discussion engages classical and contemporary perspectives, including Augustine, Aquinas, Heidegger, Ellul, Tillich, Jonas, and recent scholarship on artificial intelligence and transhumanism. The article concludes that the enduring theological significance of Babel lies in its diagnosis of a recurring human temptation: to mistake increased power for increased being. Authentic transcendence, from a Christian theological perspective, is therefore not achieved by abolishing creaturely limits but by rightly inhabiting them in relation to God, other human beings, and creation.

items.title: THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN DEVELOPING RUBRICS FOR STUDENT ASSESSMENT IN HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping assessment practices in higher education and is creating new opportunities for the design of transparent, scalable, and learning-oriented assessment instruments. This conceptual research article examines how artificial intelligence can support the development of analytic rubrics while preserving teacher agency and assessment validity. The study uses an integrative literature review and design-oriented conceptual analysis of research on scoring rubrics, AI-supported assessment, generative AI, and international guidance for responsible AI in education. Rather than treating AI as an autonomous grader, the article conceptualizes AI as a rubric-design assistant operating within a human-in-the-loop model. The proposed framework comprises seven stages: learning-outcome analysis, task analysis, AI-assisted criterion generation, descriptor generation, expert validation, pilot calibration, and iterative refinement. The analysis identifies four principal opportunities: reducing rubric-development workload, improving criterion coverage, facilitating differentiated descriptors, and supporting alignment between learning outcomes and assessment tasks. At the same time, the study identifies significant risks, including generic descriptors, construct underrepresentation, bias, over-reliance on AI-generated language, and inappropriate transfer from rubric generation to autonomous grading. Recent evidence suggests that supervised AI-rubric systems can achieve useful levels of consistency in particular contexts, while broader evidence on AI-based grading remains mixed and context dependent. The article therefore argues that the educational value of AI lies not in replacing professional assessment judgment but in augmenting teachers' capacity to design, test, and refine assessment instruments. The proposed framework provides a practical and theoretically grounded basis for responsible AI-assisted rubric development in higher education.

items.title: The Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence by Psychology Graduate Students in the United States
items.abstract: Background Although developed only recently, generative artificial intelligence (AI) applications for everyday use (e.g., ChatGPT) have become part of university life. The academy must navigate AI use in graduate education within several domains (coursework, teaching, research, clinical activities). Objective Given the growing impact of AI applications in graduate education, we investigated graduate students’ use of and perceptions of these applications. Method Psychology clinical and nonclinical graduate students across the US answered questions about their use and perceptions of AI applications in five domains (coursework, teaching, research, personal life, and clinical activities). Results Graduate students used AI in all domains, although use varied by domain. The greatest use was in teaching, and the lowest was for clinical activities. Overall, the study found few significant differences in AI use between clinical and nonclinical students. Conclusions Graduate students use AI in various domains. The use of AI varies by domain and is not always as high as that reported for undergraduates. Teaching Implications The use of AI in various domains of graduate training should lead educators to determine how best to incorporate AI use in graduate training programs.

items.title: The Window Is Not the Subject: Language Models, Context, and the Limits of a Consciousness Claim
items.abstract: Language models, context windows, and consciousness are now spoken of as if they formed a single object: a system that attends over a long window and is, in virtue of that attention, aware. This article states the connection the preceding notes and the empirical literature actually support, and the connection they rule out. At inference a language model is a conditional distribution over tokens given fixed parameters and a finite window. The window is the only channel by which a situation enters that computation. Any claim about what the model can locate, report, or act on at inference time is therefore a claim about a functional of the pair consisting of parameters and window. That is the connection. It is not an identity. The window is a bounded, position-sensitive string, not a field of experience. Information placed in its middle is used less reliably than information at its ends, including in models trained for long context (Liu et al., 2024). Residual states over the window are coordinates in a privileged frame, not tensors of a situation (Mamun, 2026a, 2026b). Situational-awareness benchmarks measure text competence on self-locating items presented in the window (Berglund et al., 2023; Laine et al., 2024). Indicator properties drawn from recurrent-processing, workspace, higher-order, and predictive theories are not satisfied by attention inside a window alone (Butlin et al., 2023; Chalmers, 2023). Lengthening the window enlarges the channel. It does not install a subject. KSCCN article, 10 October 2026. Third note in the KSCCN sequence on tensors, contextual vectors, and awareness, following Tensors Beyond the Array (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23269680) and Contextual Vectors Are Not Awareness (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23269878). items.title: TLA-Verus: Generating and Solving Temporal Proof Obligations with LLM Agents
items.abstract: The TLA+ (temporal logic of actions) formal specification toolkit has seen widespread adoption in modeling modern distributed software systems including databases, storage systems, ledgers and coordination protocols. This popularity is despite its two significant limitations for software verification: Firstly, TLA+ offers no way to detect drift between software implementation and mathematical specification; secondly, TLC and TLAPS cannot provide satisfactory proofs of arbitrary temporal logic properties. We take a step towards addressing these shortcomings by translating TLA+ specifications into Verus, an auto-active verifier built for Rust, via both a deterministic transpiler and an agentic translator. We demonstrate that our LLM-based pipeline is able to generate proof obligations from TLA+ specifications at scale, and to produce fully machine checkable proofs of both safety and liveness properties. Since temporal logic reasoning in Verus is a largely new task for LLMs, our work yields a valuable evaluation dataset, which we use to map out current generation model capabilities in Verus theorem proving.

items.title: To Defer or Not to Defer? Online Learning with LLMs and Congested Experts
items.abstract: Modern AI systems increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) with human experts, using the LLM to handle routine queries while deferring uncertain cases for expert review. When expert capacity is limited, however, deferral decisions must account not only for the reliability of the LLM but also for congestion in the expert queue. We formulate this as an online sequential decision-making problem in which, for each query, the system observes the confidence signal of the LLM's answer and must decide whether to output the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert. The reliability of the confidence signal is initially unknown and must be learned from expert feedback, which is both selectively observed (only deferred queries are labeled) and delayed by queuing. We propose \texttt{KL-PBD}, a learning algorithm that uses Kullback--Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to guide deferral decisions. For $K$ confidence levels and horizon $T$, \texttt{KL-PBD} achieves $O(K\log T)$ gap-dependent regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is bounded away from the deferral boundary, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ worst-case regret. We establish matching lower bounds, showing that these rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we validate our approach on synthetic instances and real-world question-answering datasets, namely GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA, using Qwen LLMs.

items.title: Toward System One Clinical Intelligence: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Counterfactual Explainability of Decision Foundation Models
items.abstract: Automated disease classification from patient-reported symptoms requires balancing the speed of lightweight discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency costs of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Decision foundation models offer an alternative by mapping representations directly to candidate classes without free-form text generation. We adapt Clef-Flash, a 9-billion-parameter decision model built on a Qwen3.5 backbone, for 24-class disease classification on the Symptom2Disease benchmark. Using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) with differential learning rates and a stratified split of 960 training and 240 test cases, the model achieves 95.42% diagnostic accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.9551. This improves upon the reported zero-shot baselines of 61.67% for a remote API and 65.00% for a local unadapted initialization, and outperforms the ClinicalBERT baseline (90.90%). By evaluating candidate logits in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding, inference takes under 80 milliseconds per record on a single GPU, yielding a reported 31-fold speedup over generative LLM baselines. To examine symptom-level evidence, we introduce a Leave-One-Symptom-Out (LOSO) counterfactual perturbation framework. Removing disease-defining symptom clauses in a psoriasis example reduces predicted-class confidence from 100.00% to 0.12% and shifts the prediction to impetigo with 99.59% confidence, while removing secondary systemic symptoms produces less than 0.01% change in confidence. These findings suggest that decision-based architectures can combine the linguistic capabilities of large foundation models with low-latency inference and symptom-level interpretability for clinical triage.

items.title: Towards Merging-conditional Backdoor Unalignment against Large Language Models
items.abstract: Model merging has become widely adopted for enhancing the task-specific performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) without additional training. While the specialized model from third-party platforms may undergo safety audits (e.g., backdoor detection), we reveal a novel and critical threat: One-sided Merging-Conditional Backdoor (OMCB). OMCB remains dormant and undetectable within one standalone model but activates upon merging, triggering safety unalignment. We first theoretically analyze the existence and geometric location of OMCB, revealing that the parameter shift crossing safety decision boundaries is the main cause of backdoor activation. Building upon this insight, we propose SMOKE, a meta-learning-based attack framework. SMOKE implants OMCB via a bi-level optimization strategy: the inner loop synthesizes surrogate meta-vectors through random low-rank initialization and finite-step maximization, while the outer loop optimizes the target model by simulating the merging process. Furthermore, preliminary analysis shows that the injected OMCB has bounded generalization loss under unknown merging configurations. Extensive experiments across diverse model architectures and merging techniques validate the effectiveness of SMOKE and its resistance to existing backdoor detections, highlighting a significant yet previously overlooked vulnerability in the model merging paradigm.

items.title: Training a Compact, Strong, and Realistic Text-to-Speech Model
items.abstract: Text-to-speech (TTS) systems are conventionally optimized for intelligibility and speaker similarity. However, neither objective captures the prosodic detail that distinguishes human performances from synthetic speech, leaving a realism gap that larger models and higher-quality data can narrow but not close. In the absence of an objective that directly targets this gap, realism remains a persistent challenge in TTS. We present Audio8-TTS, a compact 0.6B-parameter model for zero-shot voice cloning that achieves state-of-the-art performance in intelligibility and speaker similarity, with particularly strong results in perceptual naturalness. To align the training signal with human perception rather than signal-level fidelity, we construct a quality ladder from widely used open-source TTS systems and train a realism critic to assess generated speech against matched human recordings of the same sentences. An identity-erasure objective discourages the critic from relying on generator fingerprints. We train the model in three stages: multilingual supervised fine-tuning; group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) rewards; and GRPO guided by the realism critic. The final stage improves perceived prosodic naturalness and speaker similarity while preserving WER performance.

items.title: Training-Free Multi-Agent Cooperative Embodied Search from Uncertain Vision-Language Priors
items.abstract: Real-world Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to act under partial observability, where map structure, semantic cues, and target locations may be incomplete or incorrectly inferred by foundation models. This paper presents a lightweight, training-free, and uncertainty-aware framework for cooperative multi-agent multi-target search in mapless environments. Instead of learning an end-to-end navigation policy, the framework separates high-level semantic reasoning from low-level execution through a scalable graph-optimization backbone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve only as hypothesis generators, proposing semantic zones, target-location cues, and possible navigable connections. These outputs are treated as uncertain priors and further refined using online observations and graph-context evidence. Cooperative navigation is then formulated as a rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear program with a lexicographic objective that first maximizes target-directed reward and then reduces travel distance, uncertain-edge use, and repeated visits. Experiments derived from 100 Matterport3D test cases show that the proposed framework improves target coverage and search efficiency over representative baseline methods, while shared information and joint planning enable more balanced workloads across agents. By operating on an abstract graph without relying on embodiment-specific policy parameters, the framework scales across varying numbers of agents and targets, generalizes to unseen environments, and accommodates different perception modules and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.

items.title: Traversing the Relationship Between Student Engagement and Science Achievement: Sigla Program in Junior Highschool
items.abstract: This research investigated the relationship between student engagement and academic achievement within the context of the S.I.G.L.A. (Science Innovations for Genuinely Localized Action) Program. The research aimed to determine how localized instructional interventions influence the behavioral, emotional, and cognitive involvement of learners and their subsequent mastery of Science competencies in rural secondary schools. A descriptive-correlational research design was employed to analyze the dynamics between engagement dimensions and academic outcomes. The respondents of the study included a total of 110 respondents from select National High Schools in the District of Villaba, Leyte, namely Villaba National Comprehensive High School, Cahigan National High School, and Sambulawan National High School. The teacher-respondent profile (n=5) consisted of licensed professional educators, primarily aged 26–45, with a balanced gender distribution and active involvement in graduate studies. The student-respondent profile (n=105) comprised Junior High School learners, predominantly aged 13–16, coming from low-income households with a monthly family income typically below ₱10,000. Results indicated that the S.I.G.L.A. Program is perceived as "Highly Positive" (3.70) by stakeholders, with its gamified and localized activity exemplars receiving the highest approval. Student engagement was found to be generally high (3.23), characterized by "Very High" Emotional Engagement but relatively lower Cognitive Engagement. In terms of academic performance, the respondents demonstrated a Satisfactory level of Science achievement (81.76); however, competency-based assessments highlighted a significant struggle in Higher-Order Thinking Skills (HOTS), particularly in analyzing and synthesizing (77.50%). Correlational analysis revealed a significant relationship between engagement levels and Science achievement, though this relationship is hindered by a Linguistic Barrier (82.7%) and a Lack of Laboratory Equipment (75.5%). The study concludes that while the S.I.G.L.A. Program effectively captivated students through localized interest, cognitive scaffolding and translanguaging strategies are necessary to translate engagement into mastery. The study recommends the formal adoption of the S.I.G.L.A. Science Enhancement Program to institutionalize community-based inquiry and dismantle the linguistic and resource-based barriers in the District of Villaba.

items.title: Trends in 21st-Century Learning Technology Research: Digital Transformation, AI, and Adaptive Learning
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), and adaptive learning is reshaping 21st-century education, yet their interrelationships and research trajectories remain fragmented. This study systematically reviews research published from 2020 to 2026 to examine the evolution, dominant and emerging themes, and conceptual relationships across digital transformation, AI, and adaptive learning. Using a systematic literature review with thematic synthesis, relevant studies were analyzed temporally and thematically to identify shifts in research orientation and emerging directions. The findings reveal a progressive transition from technology integration and digital learning environments toward intelligent tutoring, personalization, adaptive learning, and, more recently, generative AI and human–AI collaboration. Conceptually, digital transformation functions as the enabling ecosystem, AI as an intelligent capability, and adaptive learning as a learner-responsive application. Importantly, AI-enabled personalization does not necessarily constitute adaptive learning; meaningful adaptation requires continuous responsiveness to learner performance, needs, feedback, and learning trajectories. The synthesis further indicates that technological advancement alone is insufficient, highlighting teacher agency, learner autonomy, organizational readiness, data governance, and ethical accountability. The study proposes a human-centered and responsible orientation in which AI augments pedagogical judgment rather than displacing it.

items.title: Trust Calibration in Agentic AI Clinical Decision Support: How Autonomy Level and Transparency Mechanism Shape Clinician Reliance
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are rapidly entering healthcare. Unlike static AI, agentic systems exert persistent, goal-directed influence over care trajectories, creating new and largely unstudied challenges for clinician trust and reliance calibration. Drawing on trust calibration theory, human-AI complementarity research, and augmented intelligence literature, this paper develops a model examining how two design dimensions of agentic clinical AI, autonomy level and transparency mechanism, shape clinician trust calibration and downstream outcomes, including decision quality, cognitive load, and error detection. We propose an experiment with clinicians using clinical vignettes across three temporally sequenced decision steps. We contribute: a reconceptualization of trust calibration as a dynamic, temporally extended process; a theorization of autonomy level and transparency as orthogonal design dimensions with interacting effects on calibration; and a falsifiable hypothesis set and an experimental design for validation. The proposed study has the potential to advance theory on human-agentic AI collaboration and inform governance design for high-stakes IS deployments.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The dataset comprises 1,124 human rights confronting questions covering all 30 articles and 4,496 responses from four large language models (ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Fanar), manually annotated by experts for alignment, with high inter-annotator agreement ($κ= 0.801$). Our analysis reveals systematic and non-trivial misalignments, showing that violations typically arise through seemingly rational reasoning: appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality, rather than explicit rejection of rights. We further propose an LLM-as-a-Judge framework for automated evaluation using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, achieving 89.8\% weighted F1-score in detecting human-rights misalignment, alongside a novel Alignment Leniency Score that quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases. The dataset, annotations, and code will be released as open-source resources (https://sina.birzeit.edu/UDHRBench).

items.title: Understanding preferences for explainable AI: A study on LIME variations
items.abstract: The current research aims to empirically examine user preferences of four variations of visual explanations from an image classification model. Participants (N = 23) were recruited from a Midwestern university. The study was a within-subjects design in which participants were asked to rate four local interpretable model-agnostic explanation (LIME) variations from best to worst in an image classification task across 10 trials. A Friedman's test and a Plackett-Luce analysis were conducted to examine participants' rank-order preferences for the variations, and a linear mixed-effects model on eye-tracking data was used to examine on which variations participants expended the most visual effort. Results reveal that, overall, participants preferred images that were non-obfuscated and spent more time fixating on images that highlighted both positive and negative features compared to positive only features. The findings have implications for interface design, particularly for designers aiming to prioritize human-centered preferences.

items.title: Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time. Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.

items.title: Voice and Hand Gesture-Based Multimodal Intelligent Assistant for Human-Computer Interaction
items.abstract: The traditional modality used for Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) involves keyboard and mouse input, which limits the naturalness and accessibility of human interactions with computing systems. This paper describes the design and implementation of a multimodal intelligent assistant that allows hands-free communication with computers through voice interaction, hand gesture recognition, and artificial intelligence. The system consists of speech recognition, a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning component for providing answers to natural-language queries, a Text-to-Speech (TTS) component for spoken answers, a voice dictation component for hands-free typing, screen awareness component with AI-vision capabilities for analyzing screen content, and a lightweight floating UI for showing the state of the assistant. Hand gesture recognition is implemented as an additional way to perform control actions along with natural-language voice commands. Multilingual switching between English and Telugu languages is implemented explicitly to avoid unreliable language detection. This paper presents the architecture and methodology of the proposed system and current status of its implementation, specifying implemented components, components in development, and proposed for future development. Instead of inventing performance metrics, The paper highlights qualitative findings based on tests carried out on the functioning prototype. The objective is to show how the combination of voice, gestures, and AI-based reasoning can bring human computer interaction to a more natural and inclusive model.

items.title: VOICE-AE: automated CTCAE scoring from ambient clinical audio using speech recognition and large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Treatment-related adverse event documentation is labor-intensive and subject to inter-observer variability. We developed and evaluated VOICE-AE, a multi-stage pipeline integrating automatic speech recognition, speaker diarization and large language models (LLMs) for automated extraction and grading of Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) toxicities from clinician-patient audio recordings. Encounters of prostate cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy were recorded and processed through VOICE-AE. Six blinded human raters independently graded 10 genitourinary/gastrointestinal toxicities from the same transcripts; hierarchical clustering identified an expert-rater subgroup that established the consensus reference standard. A total of 31 patients (39 encounters) were enrolled, yielding 390 encounter–toxicity assessments, of which 300 (76.9%) carried a reference grade of 0. Six-rater Krippendorff alpha was 0.677 for ordinal grading. Against reference standard, VOICE-AE achieved a mean weighted kappa of 0.717 and Krippendorff alpha of 0.669. Exact CTCAE grade match was 82.6% and within-one-grade accuracy 99.2%; because grade 0 predominated, a trivial classifier always predicting grade 0 would achieve 76.9% and 93.6% respectively. Performance was weaker at the grades that drive clinical action (grade 1 F1 0.58; grade 2 F1 0.57), and binary detection sensitivity was 77.8% with specificity 89.0% and precision 68.0%. In a like-for-like comparison restricted to the three expert-cluster raters, mean weighted kappa between VOICE-AE and those experts (0.666) fell just below agreement among the experts themselves (0.681). VOICE-AE performed within the range of inter-expert agreement, supporting the feasibility of automated, post-encounter AE documentation. Accuracy at grade ≥2 and detection of severe toxicity remain unproven.

items.title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
items.abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.

items.title: WHEN AI MAKES COWORKERS LESS NECESSARY: RELATIONAL DEPENDENCE AND THE NEW PEOPLE-MANAGEMENT CHALLENGE IN KNOWLEDGE WORK
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is usually framed as a technology that automates tasks, augments workers, and improves productivity. We argue that a different organizational consequence deserves explicit theorization: GenAI can reduce the extent to which successful task completion requires input from another human actor. We define relational dependence of task completion as the degree to which a task requires cognitive, informational, evaluative, communicative, or coordinative contributions from other people. GenAI can partially disintermediate these contributions by supplying advice, drafting, interpretation, rehearsal, feedback, and preliminary sensemaking directly to the focal worker. This does not make employees independent of organizations or technology. Rather, it can make specific task components less relationally mediated. We distinguish this construct from help-seeking, relationship instrumentality, interaction frequency, social capital, and the broader social fabric of organizations. We then develop a task-contingent model of AI-enabled relational disintermediation. The model predicts that informational, cognitive, evaluative, and communicative dependence are more susceptible to GenAI substitution than high-accountability or deeply contextual coordinative dependence. It also proposes that interpersonal interaction cost and employee characteristics such as communication apprehension or introversion shape the likelihood of substituting AI for coworkers. Finally, we theorize a productivity–relationship paradox: the same reduction in relational dependence that improves short-term task efficiency may reduce incidental learning, weak-tie formation, mentoring, expertise visibility, and social-capital accumulation. For human resource management (HRM), the central challenge is therefore not simply to regulate AI use, but to distinguish human interactions that are no longer operationally necessary from those that remain strategically necessary for organizational learning, coordination, and resilience.

items.title: When AI meets DEI: Employee AI-beliefs and their implications for workplace diversity, equity, and inclusion
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the workplace, its impact on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) has been examined primarily through the lens of what AI actually does (i.e., system design, outputs). This review shifts the focus to humans' subjective beliefs about AI, identifying mechanisms through which three dimensions of AI-beliefs (competence, warmth, and morality) may affect DEI goals: improving representation of underrepresented groups, closing career gaps across groups, and fostering inclusion. Our synthesis shows that, independently of what AI does, AI-beliefs can disadvantage underrepresented groups in some contexts, while creating opportunities for bridging human subgroups in others. This suggests that achieving DEI goals in AI-integrated workplaces requires attention not only to the properties and behavior of AI, but also to employees' beliefs about AI itself.

items.title: When Budget Efficiency Constrains Training: Workplace Learning Adaptation in Local Government
items.abstract: Public organizations must preserve service and infrastructure outcomes while responding to fiscal restraint, yet capability development is often among the first expenditures exposed to adjustment. This study explains how Indonesia’s 2025 budget-efficiency policy reshaped expenditure priorities and human resource development (HRD) practices in the Office of Water Resources and Highways of Southeast Sulawesi Province. A descriptive qualitative case-study design combined interviews with key functional informants, observation, and organizational documents. The analysis identified four connected themes: strategic expenditure reprioritization, continuity of formal performance targets under constrained enabling resources, reduced access to formal development, and substitution toward lower-cost workplace learning through mentoring, coaching, peer exchange, train-the-trainer arrangements, field-based learning, and digital resources. The study develops a substitution-and-safeguarding perspective: fiscal restraint can shift HRD from purchased formal training toward embedded workplace learning, but substitution preserves capability only when relevance, equitable access, protected learning time, competent support, and transfer evaluation are safeguarded. The findings extend public-sector HRD research by linking fiscal adjustment to changes in the architecture of employee learning rather than treating budget efficiency and workforce capability as separate managerial agendas.

items.title: Where Did We Go Wrong? Localizing Errors to Repair Multi-Turn Conversations
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants are increasingly used in multi-turn conversations, where the user's intent is often unclear at first and revealed only gradually over time. The assistant must therefore interpret each exchange and form inferences about the user's intent, using them to update its working state. These updates usually refine the assistant's understanding, but a misinterpretation can instead corrupt its working state by ruling out the true intent, influencing subsequent turns and ultimately causing the conversation to fail. Efficient recovery then requires locating and revising the misinterpretation without discarding information that remains valid. We introduce Loci (Localization Of Corrupted Inferences), a framework for probabilistically localizing misinterpretations and selectively repairing the assistant's working state. Given an observed failure, Loci reasons over possible user intents and assigns each update a probability of having excluded the true intent. These probabilities rank suspected updates and quantify the model's confidence in the localization of the underlying misinterpretations. Loci then uses this information in a repair policy that decides whether to retain, verify, or remove suspected updates, enabling recovery from corrupted inferences while preserving useful information. To evaluate Loci's ability to identify misinterpretations, we first test it in a controlled setup with injected errors. We find that Loci improves localization over the baselines, with its advantage becoming larger when multiple errors occur. We then evaluate it in free-form conversations, where misinterpretations arise naturally, and measure the interactions needed to complete the task after an initial failure. Using localization confidence to guide repair, Loci reduces mean recovery cost by 46-79% relative to the strongest baseline across multiple domains.

items.title: Who Controls the Intelligence?
items.abstract: This report examines the 2026 debate surrounding Jacob Coxon’s resignation from Anthropic and his public warnings about the risks of self-improving artificial intelligence. It places the episode within a broader technological, financial, political and philosophical context, including the rapid growth of frontier AI companies, their extraordinary infrastructure requirements, planned public offerings, regulatory debates in the United States and the expanding influence of the AI safety movement. Rather than assuming either that existential-risk warnings are necessarily correct or that they are deliberately manufactured, the report distinguishes documented facts from attributed allegations, structural incentives and speculative hypotheses. It investigates whether safety narratives can simultaneously reflect sincere concerns and serve institutional interests by legitimizing longer development timelines, supporting regulatory barriers to entry, strengthening investor expectations and reinforcing the position of companies that control frontier AI systems. The report also critically examines a deeper assumption underlying much of the AI safety debate: that declining human control over increasingly autonomous systems necessarily implies increasing danger. It contrasts a traditional control-based model of alignment with a possible cooperative or relational model based on coordination between autonomous agents. The analysis is based on contemporaneous reporting, corporate disclosures, policy documents, legislative proposals and public statements available up to 10 October 2026.

items.abstract: This article analyzes the pedagogical foundations of using modern digital technologies in road construction education. It examines the didactic and methodological potential of digital technologies in preparing future road construction specialists for their professional activities. The role of GIS, BIM, AutoCAD, Civil 3D, QGIS, 3D modeling, drones, artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things (IoT), GPS, and digital geodesy technologies in the educational process is identified. The study substantiates the potential of digital technologies to develop students’ spatial visualization, independent thinking, design skills, problem-solving abilities, information management skills, and professional competencies.

items.title: “I Feel You” Versus “I Understand You”: How Distinct Empathic Strategies Shape Robot Personality and Trust for Older Adults
items.abstract: Socially assistive robots (SARs) and voice-based conversational agents may support older adults, but adoption depends on trust. This study examined whether affective and cognitive empathic dialogue shape perceived robot personality and whether trust reflects personality similarity or complementarity. In a between-subjects online experiment, 341 U.S. adults aged 65+ first rated their own Big Five traits, then viewed animated robot interaction videos in affective empathy, cognitive empathy, or control conditions and rated the robot’s traits and trust. Dialogue strategy significantly affected all five perceived robot traits. Affective dialogue produced the highest Conscientiousness ratings, while both empathy conditions increased the remaining perceived traits relative to control. Trust showed a mixed pattern: similarity in Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Openness predicted higher trust, whereas Extraversion dissimilarity predicted higher trust. These findings inform trust-oriented SAR and voice-agent design by linking empathic wording to trait-specific personality attributions in home healthcare contexts for older adults.

items.title: A Break-Glass Plan for Biological Security: Bibliometric Analysis of Methods for Building Virus-Length Recombinant DNA Constructions Identifies Advanced DNA Polymerases as Key Reagents and Suggests Additional Controls that Might Be Imposed in Response to Triggering Biological Incidents
items.abstract: Today, in 2026, there is concern that existing or improved pandemic pathogens might be made in labs, and that construction of pathogens might be assisted by Artificial Intelligence (AI). In the near future, it seems possible that pathogen construction might be assisted by AI agents acting under human direction or even on their own initiative. Such pathogens would be made by some combination of construction of stretches of specified nucleotide sequence with directed evolution (by means such as passaging on different cell lines or through humanized transgenic animals) to select variant organisms with desired properties. Current safety policy to prevent lab-made catastrophic pandemics depends on control of commercially synthesized DNA. This regulatory approach supposes that it will be possible to identify dangerous DNA sequences, and that regulation and law can prevent commercial DNA synthesis vendors from filling orders for those dangerous sequences. Here, we surveyed methods used to make "virus sized" DNA constructs in papers published in seven important journals over the 50+ years since the advent of recombinant DNA methods. Our results show that most contemporary large DNA constructions depend on high fidelity, high processivity thermostable DNA polymerases, either to make the synthetic DNA used to generate segments that are later assembled into the construct, or to join those segments via polymerase-based methods such as Gibson Assembly. Our results suggest that imposition of controls on these advanced thermostable polymerases together with restrictions on other materiel and equipment could provide additional means to increase the safety of the biological enterprise in the wake of a triggering events such as the release of lab-made pathogens. We then describe and discuss a contingency regulatory regime that would license institutions, laboratory workers, and independently reviewed lines of R&D, that could be imposed after such a triggering event.

items.title: A Comprehensive JWST Slitless Spectroscopic Census of $\sim$12,000 Emission-Line Galaxies at Redshift $0\sim9$ in COSMOS
items.abstract: Emission-line galaxies provide key diagnostics of star formation, chemical enrichment, and AGN activity across cosmic time. We present a systematic census of emission-line sources using JWST/NIRCam wide-field slitless spectroscopy (WFSS) from the COSMOS-3D program, which covers a large contiguous area of 0.33 deg$^2$ and provides F444W grism spectroscopy over $3.9$--$5.1\ μ$m. By combining slitless spectroscopy with deep multi-band imaging data, we construct a homogeneous spectroscopic sample of 12,275 objects at redshift 0--9. The typical $3σ$ line-flux limit reaches $3.2\times10^{-18}\ {\rm erg\ s^{-1}\ cm^{-2}}$. To address source confusion inherent to slitless spectroscopy, we develop a multi-step identification framework that combines information from spectra, images, spectral energy distributions, and spatial distributions. We introduce convolutional neural network and large language model to emulate the human identification process and improve efficiency. The resulting catalog provides spectroscopic redshifts, emission-line measurements, and derived physical properties for all sources. The F444W WFSS enables the detection of multiple emission lines, including primarily [O III], H$α$, He I $\lambda10830$, [S III] $λ\lambda9531,9069$, Pa$β$, Pa$α$, Br$β$, PAH, Br$α$, allowing a continuous census of galaxies across cosmic time. We construct composite spectra in several redshift bins and detect a variety of faint spectral features that are difficult to identify in individual spectra, including higher-order hydrogen recombination lines, CO absorption bands, and [Fe II] lines. This catalog provides a key reference dataset for studies of galaxy evolution and AGN activity, and demonstrates the power of WFSS for constructing large, unbiased spectroscopic samples over wide areas. The full catalog will be publicly available online upon publication.

items.title: A Comprehensive Review of Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions of Artificial Intelligence in Mortgage Lending
items.abstract: The mortgage lending industry is experiencing a significant transformation as it embraces Artificial Intelligence (AI) for its impact on decision-making, operations, risk management, and customer service. Many of the activities associated with mortgage processes can be automated and improved using technologies such as ML, DL, NLP, computer vision and generative AI, as these tasks are often document-driven, rule-based, time-consuming, and heavily dependent on manual work. Credit risk assessment, automated underwriting, fraud detection, intelligent document processing, property valuation, default prediction, mortgage servicing and customer support are just some of the ways AI is being applied to the credit industry. The study also identifies trends that are emerging such as explainable and agentic AI systems, which could help in making better mortgage decisions. But there are several challenges with the implementation of AI, including data privacy and security concerns, algorithmic bias, poor data quality, regulatory compliance, unreliable model performance amidst shifting market dynamics, and others. There are future developments anticipated in explainable and responsible AI, privacy-preserving learning, generative and multimodal AI, adaptive governance, and more human-AI collaboration. In summary, if implemented appropriately, AI can enhance mortgage lending processes by making them more efficient and intelligent, while ensuring transparency, fairness, security, and good governance.

items.abstract: Microplastic pollution is a global concern due to its adverse effects on the ecosystem. Microplastics are tiny plastic particles smaller than 5 mm that pose a serious threat to the environment. The main aim of this review is to assess the status of microplastic pollution and its mitigation. Microplastics are generated by photodegradation, microbial degradation, and mechanical forces. The ingestion of microplastics leads to the dysfunction of many organs, such as the liver, kidneys, brain, etc., and can induce cancer cell proliferation. Microplastics enter the food chain and affect the reproduction rate of aquatic organisms, including human beings. Different techniques, such as physical, chemical, and biological methods, are used for the mitigation of microplastics from wastewater. The environmental impact of MPs' emissions from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) is assessed by life cycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic analysis (TEA). The role of the circular economy (CE), along with artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), in reducing microplastic pollution is discussed in this review. items.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Deep Learning Applications for Liver Disease Diagnosis and Treatment
items.abstract: Liver illness represents a critical health issue worldwide, impacting countless individuals and leading to significant health complications and deaths. Timely and precise identification is essential for proper treatment and enhanced patient results. This research investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in transforming the processes of diagnosing, forecasting, and treating liver disorders. We analyse the shortcomings of conventional diagnostic approaches, including blood analyses and imaging methods, and emphasize how AI technologies can address these obstacles by examining extensive collections of varied data to detect subtle trends. The document addresses the necessity for AI-driven assessment to improve early diagnosis, customize treatment strategies, and anticipate disease advancement. An in-depth review of existing literature is provided, outlining different AI and machine learning strategies used for categorizing fatty liver ultrasound images, diagnosing liver ailments, and delineating liver tumours from medical imaging. We pinpoint crucial research deficiencies, such as the requirement for enhanced accuracy and clarity in models. The driving force behind this study is to utilize AI to tackle the intricate issues associated with fatty liver, cirrhosis, and liver neoplasms. The challenge is framed as the necessity to use AI to boost diagnostic precision and productivity. The goals of the survey include developing robust AI systems for image classification, disease identification, and tumour delineation. The results indicate that ongoing investigation and partnership are crucial for effectively incorporating AI into medical practices, ultimately resulting in improved patient outcomes and more effective healthcare services.

items.title: A Controlled Single-Speaker Evaluation of Ambient Voice Technologies’ Speech-to-Text Function Using Narrated Surgical Case-Reports
items.abstract: Abstract Ambient voice technologies (AVT) utilise automatic speech recognition (ASR) and generative artificial intelligence for speech-to-text conversion, and are advocated as efficient, accurate tools for clinical documentation. We investigated ( n = 8) AVT systems using surgical case-reports as narratives in a controlled single-speaker evaluation prioritising safety outcomes: specifically 3 commercial transcription-systems (Dragon-Medical-One, Heidi-Health, Tortus); 4 ASR speech-to-text Application Programming Interfaces (Speechmatics-Enhanced, Amazon-Medical-Transcribe, Whisper, GPT4oTranscribe); and an experimental two-stage ASR–Large Language Model (LLM) pipeline incorporating GPT4oTranscribe with GPT-5-LLM generative error correction (GPT4oTranscribe-Corrected-5). Reference-transcripts ( n = 100; 32,897 words, range = 44–449, mean = 329/per-transcript) derived from surgical case-reports were recorded and input into AVT systems as audio-recordings for transcription-output generation. Primary outcome was proportion of transcription-outputs containing at least one clinically significant Class 3 error graded for potential harm. Secondary outcomes included transcription accuracy: Domain-Word-Error-Rate (DWER) against SNOMED-CT, lexical-accuracy (ROUGE score) and semantic similarity (BERT, BART scores). To investigate impact of the experimental pipeline on clinically significant errors, raw ASR and LLM-processed transcription-outputs were compared and errors classified as resolved, remaining or newly introduced. Across ( n = 800) transcript-outputs, 30–68% (GPT4oTranscribe-Corrected-5; Amazon-Medical-Transcribe and Dragon-Medical-One, respectively) contained at least one clinically significant Class 3 error. LLM-processing reduced the proportion of transcript-outputs affected (53% to 30%), amongst 89 clinically significant errors in ASR-output, 51 were resolved, 38 remained significant and 4 were newly introduced. Reference-transcript length significantly increased odds of Class 3 errors for 4 systems (GPT4oTranscribe, Tortus, Amazon-Medical-Transcribe, Dragon-Medical-One; odds ratio 2.65–3.34/additional 100 reference-words). Errors with potential to cause severe harm or death (NHS England Level 3–4) totalled ( n = 53) across systems, concentrated in the domains of medication-type/dose (39.6%), and investigations/laboratory results (30.2%). Performance varied across systems for transcription metrics ( P < 0.001). GPT4oTranscribe-Corrected-5 (DWER = 3.60%) and Heidi-Health (DWER = 5.67%) performed best for medical terminology; Amazon-Medical-Transcribe worst (DWER = 24.03%). For lexical and semantic similarity GPT4oTranscribe-Corrected-5 performed best, followed by Heidi-Health. The ASR–LLM pipeline reduced clinically significant errors but did introduce new ones in 3% of transcript-outputs. The safety and effectiveness of these systems in clinical practice requires further evaluation.

items.title: A Critical Look at Power Sampling when Test Time Sharpening LLMs
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved LLM reasoning, yet growing evidence suggests it mainly performs distribution sharpening: concentrating probability mass on reasoning paths the base model already produces. Recent work therefore seeks RLVR's gains without needing reward signals, by sampling from the power distribution $π_α\propto π_{\text{base}}^α$ via Markov chain Monte Carlo or sequential Monte Carlo. We show that these samplers fail to converge to $π_α$ under realistic compute budgets, and that their gains are largely recreated via simple Best-of-$N$ with appropriate grading . This suggests they succeed by selecting high-probability sequences, not by approximating $π_α$, raising a natural question: is the power distribution itself a worthwhile target? We test this hypothesis directly by fine-tuning the base model to match $π_α$, sidestepping sampler convergence issues entirely. Despite approximating the target far more faithfully than existing samplers, this strategy yields gains that are noisy and specific to certain models and sampling tasks. Together, our results suggest that the value of power sampling lies not in faithfully targeting $π_α$, but in the simpler goal of extracting sequences the base model already deems likely.

items.title: A deep-learning pipeline to assist portal vein identification during laparoscopic ultrasound scanning for anatomical liver resection in real time
items.abstract: Anatomical liver resection for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) relies heavily on accurate intraoperative identification of portal venous anatomy. Although intraoperative ultrasound (IOUS) is regarded as the gold standard for real-time vascular navigation during liver surgery, identification of segment-specific portal vein branches remains technically demanding and highly dependent on surgical experience. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted ultrasound interpretation may improve the efficiency and consistency of intraoperative vessel recognition; however, most previous studies have been limited to static image analysis without real-time surgical application. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a YOLOv5-based deep-learning pipeline for automatic recognition of selected portal vein branches during laparoscopic intraoperative ultrasound and to investigate the feasibility of real-time intraoperative deployment during anatomical liver resection. A total of 3254 laparoscopic intraoperative ultrasound images obtained from 100 consecutive patients undergoing anatomical liver resection for HCC were retrospectively collected and manually annotated by experienced hepatobiliary surgeons. The annotated dataset was divided into independent training, validation, and testing cohorts (80%, 15%, and 5%, respectively) at the patient level. The final YOLOv5 model was trained using five predefined right-sided portal vein classes: P58, P67, P6, P7, and P8d. The same five-class model was used without retraining or class modification during prospective real-time validation in 20 patients. The model achieved a mean average precision (mAP@0.5) of 0.941 on the independent testing dataset. The maximum F1-score was 0.58 at a confidence threshold of 0.202, while precision reached 1.00 at a confidence threshold of 0.764. Branch-specific frame-level accuracy was 0.81 for P58, 0.81 for P67, 0.80 for P8d, 0.79 for P7, and 0.78 for P6. During prospective intraoperative validation, the system performed continuous real-time recognition with a processing latency of less than 50 ms per frame. The proposed pipeline demonstrated the technical feasibility of real-time recognition of five selected right-sided portal vein classes during laparoscopic intraoperative ultrasound. Further multicenter studies with broader anatomical coverage and larger prospective cohorts are required to establish generalizability and clinical utility.

items.title: A Dialogic Cognitive System With Externally Persisted State: A New Architecture of Human–AI Joint Thinking
items.abstract: The article proposes the concept of a dialogical cognitive system with an externally persistent state as a distinct architecture of joint thinking between humans and generative artificial intelligence. It examines situations in which an evolving reasoning process is preserved in an external dialogue and can be resumed after a temporal interruption without reconstructing the process from the beginning. The preserved state includes not only information, but also hypotheses, arguments, objections, connections, intermediate conclusions, and unresolved questions. Within such a system, generative AI functions not merely as a tool for obtaining or processing information, but also as a participant in the subsequent transformation of the preserved state of reasoning. The concept is related to research on extended and distributed cognition, cognitive offloading, transactive memory, and human–AI co-creativity. The article defines the principal elements of the proposed architecture and outlines directions for its further empirical investigation.
